Investing.com -- Bank of America sees a potential recovery in semiconductor stocks in early 2027 as improving U.S. policy clarity, corporate buybacks and relatively attractive valuations help ease concerns over artificial intelligence spending, although investors may need to wait for earnings estimate cuts before the sector finds a durable bottom.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) has already fallen 37% from its recent peak, compared with an average correction of 32% during previous downturns. The bank said indiscriminate selling driven by fears of slowing AI capital expenditure could begin to run its course by early 2027, with congressional policy developments and share repurchases helping restore confidence.

Semiconductor stocks trade at 13.7 times forward earnings, a 22% discount to the S&P 500's 17.7 times multiple. A return to the historical trough valuation of around 12 times earnings would imply at most another 12% downside, according to BofA. The bank also highlighted buyback support from Lam Research, which has a $25 billion programme, ongoing repurchases by Nvidia and Micron's planned buyback start on December 9.

Previous semiconductor downturns suggest the sector typically declines six to nine months ahead of the fundamental earnings turn, before recovering as earnings estimate reductions become reflected in valuations. The SOX has gained an average of 42% during previous recoveries after those cuts were priced in.

BofA sees the late-June 2026 market peak as a potential signal that earnings estimate reductions could begin in the first quarter of 2027, as companies adjust second-half spending plans. However, the bank cautioned that cheaper valuations alone may not be sufficient to restore confidence, with actual earnings cuts likely needed to establish a sustainable floor.

AI spending remains the biggest swing factor

U.S. cloud capital expenditure is currently running at an annualised rate of about $1.2 trillion, with forecasts pointing to more than $1.5 trillion in 2027. If spending stabilises at current levels rather than accelerating, it would represent a roughly 20% downside against 2027 capital expenditure expectations.

That scenario could reduce planned AI infrastructure deployment to around 30 gigawatts from more than 40 gigawatts in BofA's baseline assumptions. At an estimated $40 billion per gigawatt of investment, the adjustment could create substantial pressure on semiconductor revenue and earnings.

title: Bank of America has unexpected advice for tech stock investors after midterms
detail:
Bank of America has unexpected advice for tech stock investors after midterms
Moz Farooque, Aparajita Chatterjee

BAC
^NDX
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Checking your retirement account on Thursday afternoon, November 5, felt like a gut punch, with months of hard-earned gains vanishing in hours. 

Even with diversification in mind, simply holding a standard index fund left you absorbing the damage. The Nasdaq 100 erased $2.3 trillion in market value as a post-midterm panic triggered a brutal tech sell-off, Bloomberg reported. 

AI poster-children like Nvidia tumbled more than 9%, while AMD plunged over 17%. The bounce-back the next day brought brief relief but zero answers.

For years, riding Big Tech felt like a foolproof ticket to America's AI boom. Now, mounting political resistance to data centers and runaway corporate spending have investors asking if the math has permanently changed.

Bank of America has a surprising answer. Its post-election outlook uncovers a contrarian opportunity, posing an urgent question for anyone counting on the stock market for retirement.

Why Bank of America favors tech debt over tech stocks

Bank of America just dropped one of the most surprising messages for investors rattled by tech's sell-off: that owning a great tech business isn't necessarily the best way to invest in it. For now, the bank prefers tech company bonds to tech stocks.

More Wall Street:

Nvidia and Micron are about to lord their successes all over Wall Street

Nvidia, Palantir and Alphabet send waves through Wall Street

Wall Street elites will pocket windfall from record $46 billion profits

In post-midterm research, chief investment strategist Michael Hartnett favored "tech bonds over tech stocks," as reported by Seeking Alpha. Bonds pay contractual interest and generally rank ahead of common shares if a company fails. That said, they aren't risk-free, and missed payments and rising market yields can still hurt investors.

The shift goes further. BofA prefers consumer staples, represented by the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLP), to energy shares represented by XLE. It also favors smaller businesses over market giants as reported by TipRanks.

That's meaningful for retirement savers. An S&P 500 fund owns hundreds of stocks, but its largest holdings carry outsized weight, a concentration risk that veteran market commentator Jim Cramer has also warned about.

After years when giant technology firms led returns, a pullback in just a few companies can affect an otherwise diversified account.

BofA strategists raised the possibility of "peak AI equity concentration," questioning where the next dollar of investment belongs.

JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), Wells Fargo (NYSE: WFC), Citigroup (NYSE: C), Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS), and Morgan Stanley (NYSE: MS) have something in common: They're among the biggest names in American banking. But how they make their money can be surprisingly different.

Some rely heavily on traditional lending, collecting interest on mortgages, credit cards, and business loans. Others generate billions from investment banking, trading, and managing money for wealthy clients. Some do a little bit of everything.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

All six banks reported third-quarter earnings on Oct. 13 and 14, giving investors a closer look at the businesses driving their profits. Here's what stood out with these six bank stocks.

Image source: Getty Images.
JPMorgan Chase: A little bit of everything

JPMorgan Chase is the U.S.'s largest bank, and one of its biggest advantages is its ability to earn money in multiple ways. Its asset management business generated $5.9 billion in fees during Q3, a 15% increase from a year ago. Investment banking fees climbed 13% to $3 billion, including a 32% jump in advisory fees.

Don't overlook the credit card business. Card income surged 25% to $1.43 billion, helped by higher annual fees. Meanwhile, revenue from Card Services & Auto increased 15% to $8.28 billion. Even automobile leasing is contributing to growth. Operating lease income reached $1.2 billion, up from $987 million a year earlier, as the bank expanded its portfolio of leased vehicles.

That's the appeal of JPMorgan Chase's business model. It can generate revenue from everyday consumer banking while collecting substantial fees from wealthy investors and corporate clients.

Bank of America: Wealth management is doing the heavy lifting

Bank of America is another banking giant with several revenue streams, but its wealth management business has become a particularly important source of growth. Global Wealth & Investment Management generated $7.1 billion in Q3 revenue, up 13%, while net income reached $1.54 billion. Asset management fees climbed to approximately $4.5 billion from $3.9 billion a year earlier. Client balances reached a whopping $5.1 trillion.

Bank of America also makes substantial money from a business that most people rarely think about. Its Global Transaction Services operation helps companies manage payments, cash, and other financial transactions. Revenue from that business increased 11% to $3.04 billion.

Bank of America paid a big fine and kept its raise

Bank of America's lending engine is growing. Net interest income rose 8% to $16.4 billion in the third quarter of 2026 compared with a year earlier.

On Oct. 13, 2026, the Treasury Department fined Bank of America more than $1.2 billion for anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations. Third-quarter diluted EPS fell to $0.91, from $1.04 in the third quarter of 2025.

The board raised the dividend 14% in July, to $0.32 a quarter, and declared the same $0.32 on Oct. 21. Coverage is wide: 28% of normalized EPS in fiscal 2025 and 27% on fiscal 2026 consensus. Nineteen analysts expect normalized EPS to rise 18% to $4.51 in fiscal 2026.

CFO Alastair Borthwick spelled out the order on the third-quarter call: "We know we have to support the regulatory minimum and the dividend. And then whatever is left, we're going to return to shareholders." That quarter, the bank paid $2.2 billion in dividends and spent $6.0 billion on buybacks, so buybacks would give way long before the dividend did.

title: Boot Barn has a plan to win holiday shoppers, and BofA likes it
detail:
Boot Barn has a plan to win holiday shoppers, and BofA likes it
Peace Longe, Celine Provini
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 11:47 AM CST 5 min read
BOOT
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The holiday season is coming, and Boot Barn (BOOT) is getting ready for the shopping that comes with it.

Boot Barn operates more than 580 stores across 49 U.S. states, selling cowboy boots, denim, work boots, and ranch apparel. Although the stock has had a tough 2026, Wall Street wants to see whether the company can pull off a strong holiday quarter. 

BOOT shares are down about 28% this year, but the stock has increased by roughly 20% over the past five trading days. That recent bounce followed the company's second-quarter results. Bank of America then added another round of support.

In early November, BofA analyst Chris Nardone, who covers softlines and consumer retail for the bank, met with Boot Barn's management and was impressed by their plans.

Because of that and the company's recent results, he kept his Buy rating and $166 price target on BOOT. That price target implies about a 24% increase from the stock's recent $133 share price.

A women's boot refresh aimed squarely at Black Friday

Boot Barn's leadership has been clear that their women's fashion boots are a weak spot for the company. However, CEO John Hazen told BofA that the company is moving fast to fix that.

Boot Barn is bringing in more color options and higher-priced fashion styles in time for Black Friday. The company has also featured the new boots in Boot Barn's holiday gift guide and national TV ads so they can bring more shoppers into stores.

Also read: Kroger cuts discounts, promises pricing changes

Men's boots are also showing a few signs of weakness. In Boot Barn's fiscal second quarter of 2027, sales of men's rubber-soled Western boots slowed. The company's management isn't sure yet whether the reason was the warm weather or customers being more careful with their spending because of the economic situation. 

Even so, the company's management remains hopeful about the holiday season. In the company's October earnings release filed with the SEC, Hazen said Boot Barn is "excited about the holiday season," pointing to refreshed products, improved stores, and a bigger national marketing push.

Boot Barn is leaning on a refreshed women's boot assortment and a national TV ad push to drive traffic into its stores this holiday season.Darya Komarova / Getty Images
Why BofA still sees Boot Barn stock as a bargain

BofA still sees BOOT as a bargain because of its valuation. Boot Barn trades at about 14 times its expected earnings over the next two years.

Nardone thinks that's low for Boot Barn, especially since he expects the company to grow its earnings by 15% next year, once tariff refunds are stripped out. In the BofA note shared with me, Nardone described the stock as "cheap relative to its growth profile."

Tripadvisor downgraded by BofA as CEO and CFO exits add risk Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock

Tripadvisor Inc (NASDAQ:TRIP) earnings recovery could take longer than expected, Bank of America warned, downgrading the company to "underperform" from "buy" and cutting its target to $8 from $15.

The bank cited slowing growth and traffic disruption, with the CEO and CFO departing over the next few months during restructuring, adding execution risk.

Third-quarter revenue fell 11% against guidance for a 7% to 10% year-over-year decline, while revenue and EBITDA missed Wall Street expectations, according to BofA.

Tripadvisor's fourth-quarter outlook points to further weakness, with revenue guided down by a low-teens percentage versus Wall Street's expected 5% decline.

Bank of America consequently cut its fourth-quarter 2026 revenue estimate to $310 million from $332 million and EBITDA to $17 million from $40 million.

The reductions extend into its annual forecasts, with 2026 and 2027 revenue now expected to fall 9.6% and 5.0%, versus 7.5% and 1.1% previously.

BofA lowered corresponding EBITDA estimates to $180 million and $174 million from $221 million and $235 million, citing higher sales and marketing spending.

Those forecasts reflect Tripadvisor's search engine optimization and AI-driven traffic disruption, softer US-Europe demand, and increasing competition, according to Bank of America.

The bank expects search-related traffic losses through 2027, while management's growth-over-margin priority that year and greater reliance on paid marketing could delay earnings recovery.

BofA therefore remains uncertain about Viator's return to sustainable double-digit growth with improved marketing efficiency.

There are encouraging signs, however, as Bank of America said AI-referred Experiences traffic converts well despite small volumes, while management is directing product, engineering and analytics resources toward Viator.

Potential challenges to the bank's cautious view include a strategic-review outcome involving a sale or further portfolio actions.

Other upside risks include faster Experiences growth as macroeconomic and geopolitical pressures ease, AI and new paid channels scale, and restructuring and marketing efficiency support margin recovery.

BofA also cited approximately $685 million in net TheFork proceeds as providing flexibility to reduce debt and potentially resume capital returns.
